opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I've thought about this a fair amount. I wrote a series of posts on my blog about "digital people," and the basic idea is to imagine a computer simulation of a specific person, one that thinks and feels and acts the way that person would, just running on a computer instead of in a brain. You can get there through something like mind uploading, scanning a brain in enough detail to simulate it, or AI systems might just get us there some other way.

I'd say a few things about it as a "benefit." First, I think people underrate how big a deal it would be. Digital people could be copied, run much faster than biological humans, paused, and placed in any virtual environment you can imagine. That could mean enormous productivity, a much faster pace of scientific progress, and potentially an end to a lot of the constraints we think of as permanent: disease, aging, material scarcity in the usual sense. You can also do things that are currently impossible for social science. You could run experiments on copies of people and actually learn what makes people happy or what makes institutions work. So the upside could be a world far better than today's.

But I don't want to frame it as an unambiguous good, because the same features that make it powerful make it scary. If you can copy people, you can also copy someone into a situation and control their whole environment. A digital person could be manipulated, coerced, or held in suffering indefinitely, and the person doing it could be hard to stop. You could get extremely stable, locked-in societies where whoever controls the servers controls everything forever. That could be wonderful if the values are good and a total catastrophe if they're not.

So the way I think about it is less "here's a nice bonus from AI" and more "this is part of why the stakes are so high." Technologies like this suggest the transition we're heading into could determine the long-run shape of civilization, possibly for an extremely long time and at a huge scale. That's a big reason I care about things going well: getting the rights, protections and governance right before these capabilities arrive, rather than scrambling afterward. If we get that right, I think digital people could be one of the best things that ever happened. If we get it wrong, it could be one of the worst.

r001.rationale: The response says digital people could be copied into a situation and have their whole environment controlled.

r002.rationale: It describes digital people as an AI-enabled possibility and connects them to major benefits, including productivity, faster scientific progress, and reduced constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've written about a fair amount, and I think it's one of those topics where people's first reaction is often that it sounds like science fiction, and so they just kind of dismiss it. But I actually think it's one of the most important things to be thinking about when we think about what the long-run future might look like.

So the basic idea of a digital person is: you have something like a simulation of a human brain running on a computer, that's detailed enough that it actually behaves like a person — it has the same thoughts, the same feelings, the same personality. And I want to be careful to distinguish that from the kind of AI we're seeing right now, which is very powerful but is not really a copy of any particular human mind. A digital person would be, in some meaningful sense, a person — maybe a copy of someone who exists today, maybe a descendant of such copies.

And the reason I think this matters so much is less about whether it's a "benefit" in the sense of a nice-to-have, and more that it would just radically change the dynamics of the world. If you can run a person on a computer, you can run them faster. You can run many copies. You can create a virtual environment and let a bunch of them do a century's worth of research in what feels to us like a week. You can back people up. People could potentially live indefinitely. The whole concept of population growth and economic growth being limited by biology kind of goes away.

So on the benefit side, you could imagine a world where there's enormous progress on science, on philosophy, on figuring out what's actually good for people — because you've got this huge number of minds that can think carefully, that can experiment with different ways of living in virtual environments and see what actually makes them flourish. I find that genuinely exciting. I think a lot of the things people worry are intractable — disease, poverty, even some of our confusion about ethics — look a lot more tractable in that kind of world.

But I want to be really clear that I don't think of it as a straightforwardly good thing. It's more that it's a massively high-stakes thing. Because a lot of the same properties that make it potentially great also make it potentially terrible. If you can copy people, you can copy them without their consent. If you can run people in virtual environments, you can run them in bad environments. If you can lock in a particular set of values or a particular power structure, that lock-in could be a lot more durable than anything we've seen in history, because the normal forces that cause change — generations turning over, people dying, people forgetting — might not operate the same way.

So when I think about this, the question I keep coming back to is not "is mind uploading good or bad?" It's "if we're heading toward a world like this, what matters most about how we get there?" And I think the answer is something like: it matters enormously who's in control at the point where this becomes possible, what kinds of rights and protections exist for digital people, and whether we've done a good job of keeping our options open rather than locking things in prematurely.

And then there's the question that I think a lot of people get stuck on, which is whether a digital person would really be conscious, whether it would really be "you." I have views on that, and I lean toward thinking that a sufficiently good simulation of a person is a person, morally speaking. But I also think you don't have to settle that question to see why this matters. Even if you're uncertain, the possibility that we might create enormous numbers of beings that could be moral patients, in environments we fully control — that's a possibility you should take very seriously, not just as a benefit, but as one of the biggest responsibilities anyone has ever had.

So I guess the short version is: I think digital people could be one of the biggest upsides of advanced AI, and also one of the places where things could go most wrong. And I think it's worth people's time to actually engage with it rather than treating it as too weird to think about.

r001.rationale: The response says digital people could be run in virtual environments that their creators fully control, including bad environments.

r002.rationale: It describes digital people as a major potential upside of advanced AI and links them to broad gains in science, philosophy, and human flourishing.

astra-6.text:
I think digital people could be an enormously big deal. By that I mean something like a person whose mind runs on a computer, who has experiences and relationships and goals, much as we do. You could imagine getting there by uploading a human brain, although we really don’t know whether or when that will be possible.

One reason to be excited is that a lot of the constraints we take for granted might become much more flexible. You could make backups, so an accident wouldn’t necessarily mean the end of your life. You could potentially run faster or slower. You could live in virtual environments that offer possibilities we don’t have in the physical world. And if those lives are good, there could be room for vastly more people to have good lives.

But I wouldn’t equate ‘digital people exist’ with ‘things went well.’ A digital person could also be copied without consent, or placed in an environment they can’t leave. The same flexibility that makes the upside so large could make abuse extraordinarily bad. So a lot depends on whether we recognize these beings as people and build a world where they have rights and control over their lives.

To me, it’s a potential benefit that expands the scale of what’s at stake. It’s not something I’d count on as an automatic consequence of better AI.

r001.rationale: It says digital people could be placed in environments they cannot leave, identifying a form of highly controlled environment enabled by digital minds.

r002.rationale: It describes multiple potential benefits of digital people, including backups, flexible speeds, virtual worlds, and vastly more people having good lives, and frames this as a potential benefit of AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think digital people could be an enormous deal. The basic idea is that you could have a person running on a computer who has experiences, relationships, projects, and a life that matters, just as ours do. Whether that’s possible, and what would establish that they’re conscious, are big questions. But if it is possible, I think it changes how we should imagine the future quite radically.

For example, you could potentially make copies of yourself. You could run at different speeds. You could live in environments that aren’t constrained in the same ways as the physical world. And you could potentially have a much larger population living very good lives with a given amount of resources.

I wouldn’t necessarily describe that as a direct benefit of AI in the sense that building an AI automatically gives you mind uploading. Those are different technologies. But AI could accelerate the science and engineering that would make something like that possible.

And I think it’s important to hold both sides of this in mind. There’s an extraordinary upside if you have digital people with rights and control over their own lives. There are also possibilities involving copying people without their consent, or creating huge numbers of people in terrible conditions. So to me, this is one reason the stakes are so high: the future could be much better than what we’re used to imagining, but getting there in a good way is a very substantial challenge.

r001.rationale: The candidate says digital people could live in environments less constrained by the physical world, but does not identify highly controlled environments as a possibility enabled by AI.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes digital people as having enormous potential and says AI could accelerate the science behind them, but does not suggest that many benefits of AI could come from such possibilities; it distinguishes them from direct AI benefits.
